newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER SHOWCASE-JUVE-MILAN GAME SPLITS ITALY IN TWO.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-JUVE-MILAN GAME SPLITS ITALY IN TWO.

text.p: In a country that appears to pull together only when cheering on Ferrari or Alberto Tomba, the biggest soccer match of the season does nothing for the cause of Italian unity.
From Sicily to the Alps, the Juventus v AC Milan clash divides this soccer-mad nation in two.

"It's the true Italian derby," Alessandro Lanzarini of soccer weekly Guerin Sportivo told Reuters. "Juventus and Milan are the best supported clubs in the country and together can claim the allegiance of more than 50 percent of all fans."
But the Juventus-Milan split stretches beyond geography to history -- it's also about a cultural clash between two epochs.

If Milan and their owner Silvio Berlusconi represent the New Age of soccer, where television wealth holds the key to success, then Juventus and the Agnelli family, club owners for three-quarters of a century, come from a different period, when winning titles was the whim of a rich industrialist.

In the 1970s and for much of the post-war period, the finest and most loved soccer team in Italy was Juventus, owned by the Agnelli-run Fiat car-making company and based in the country's industrial capital Turin.
In the mid-1980s, Italy's footballing figurehead passed to AC Milan, run by media mogul Berlusconi whose matches are broadcast on Berlusconi-owned television channels.
To compete in the harsh new world of soccer, Juventus have had to sacrifice some of their old industrial roots and form a pact with the "red devils".

In the summer of 1995, Juve formed a joint business venture with their arch-rivals -- the two clubs agreed to work together on television and worldwide marketing to cut costs and share business strategy, especially in the Far East.
But, if anything, the Juve-Milan pax off the field has only heightened the rivalry on it.
Juventus's new business-like approach to soccer has seen them forego traditional Italian loyalty to long-serving players in the name of balancing the books.
In the past two seasons, they have sold the likes of Gianluca Vialli, Fabrizio Ravanelli and Roberto Baggio.
The sale of stars has not stopped them winning a league title and the European Cup in successive seasons, giving their annual encounter with Milan the air of a title play-off.
In the past four years, the aggregate winner of the two Juventus-Milan matches -- home and away -- has gone on to take the championship.
The rivalry between the two sides started in 1901, when Juventus lost 3-2 in the championship play-offs to a Milan side on their way to their first-ever league title.

Juventus fans also still smart about their humiliating 7-1 defeat to Milan in Turin in 1951 -- still their heaviest ever setback in serie A -- although it failed to stop them winning the league by seven points.
But for the most part, the history of Juventus and AC Milan is about trophies -- lots of them.
Their roll of honour fills pages and pages of Italian soccer history, taking in no less than 77 trophies -- 41 to Juventus and 36 to AC Milan.
In the league, Juventus dominate with 23 league championships to Milan's 15 but, unlike their rivals, the Turin club's domestic domination has rarely carried over into Europe.
Juve have won the European Cup just twice compared with five for Milan.

After 124 serie A serie encounters, however, there is little to separate the sides in terms of statistics. Juve are slightly on top with 42 wins to Milan's 39, with both side's goal difference equal: 170 for and 170 against.
Despite the parity in facts and figures, a victory for Juventus in Sunday's match would further the growing impression that the Turin side are ready to succeed Milan as the dominant force in serie A.
In the past century, Juventus and Milan's domination of Italian football has worked in "cicli" -- Italian for cycles.

In the 1930s, Juventus won five successive league titles with AC Milan way down the table. In the 1950s, it was Milan's turn with a side that included the two Swedes Gunnar Nordahl and Nils Liedholm taking them to four titles in a decade.
By the 1970s and early 80s, Juve, under Giovanni Trapattoni's guidance were dominant once more until Berlusconi launched Milan's 10 year "ciclo".
Now the balance of power is set to change again.
Berlusconi's club might have won four league titles in the past five years, including last season's championship, but there are growing signs that his side is on the wane.

Coach Oscar Washington Tabarez, brought in to replace Fabio Capello -- now with Real Madrid -- has struggled to find a settled side with Dejan Savicevic and Franco Baresi carrying injuries. The team's once solid defence has suddenly appeared porous.
As a result, they have lost three matches in eight league outings this season and lie in fifth place, five points behind serie A leaders and city rivals Inter.
By contrast, despite selling Vialli and Ravanelli in the summer, Juventus coach Marcello Lippi started the season in convincing form including a superb 2-0 victory over Inter.
The Turin club have lost their way a little in recent matches, with three victories in seven matches but a win on Sunday would give them a five-point lead over struggling Milan.
To add spice to an already mouth-watering occasion, both sides are only too aware that the encounter could be a dress rehearsal for a European Cup clash in February.

With AC Milan likely to finish runners-up in Group D and Juventus favourites to win Group C, the reigning European champions and the Italian title holders are likely to see their paths cross in the quarter-finals.
